summary: Describes how X.509 keys and signatures are identified and encoded for use in version 2 of the KeyNote trust-management system. X.509 certificates can then appear directly in KeyNote assertions, making it easier to combine the two systems. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: KeyNote is a system for deciding who is allowed to do what, and X.509 is a common form of digital ID card. This document explains how to put those ID cards into KeyNote's rules.

subtitle: How KeyNote credentials can name an X.509 certificate as a key, and which hash functions their signatures may use.

tldr.problem: KeyNote assertions identify principals by public keys, but RFC 2792 only defines RSA and DSA key and signature encodings, so protocols that already use X.509 certificates had no direct way to plug in.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lets a whole DER-encoded X.509 certificate, written out as hex or base64 text, stand in for a key. It also defines matching signature names and adds SHA256, SHA512 and RIPEMD160 signature types.
tldr.outcome: An Informational document from the Independent Submission stream. It discourages SHA1 and leaves checking certificate validity to the application developer.

today: RFC 5708 is an Informational document published through the Independent Submission stream, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC Editor makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: Why KeyNote Needs X.509 Keys
sections.content:
KeyNote is a trust-management system built around assertions: small, highly structured programs that say which actions the holders of specific public keys are allowed to perform. A signed assertion, called a credential assertion, can be sent over an untrusted network and plays the role of a certificate. See RFC 2704 for KeyNote itself; this RFC assumes the reader already knows it.

Keys in KeyNote identify principals, and implementations must convert them to a normalized form before comparing them. RFC 2792 covers RSA and DSA keys. This RFC adds a key identifier so that an X.509 certificate (RFC 5280) can be used wherever an RSA or DSA key could be, and it defines signature encodings that go with it. It also adds signature types using hash functions beyond MD5 and SHA1, which have been found vulnerable to attack in recent years.
sections.plainLanguage: KeyNote rules say which keys may do which jobs. This document lets a digital ID card stand in for a key, so systems that already use ID cards can talk to KeyNote.

sections.title: Encoding and Comparing X.509 Keys
sections.content:
An X.509 key identifier is the ASN.1 Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) encoding of the whole certificate, as defined in Section 4 of RFC 5280. For use in a KeyNote credential, that binary object is turned into ASCII text, either hex digits or base64 characters. The algorithm name written in front of it is x509-hex: or x509-base64:. Other ASCII encodings may be defined in the future.

For comparison, KeyNote takes the Subject public key out of the certificate and uses it in the normalized form from Section 2 of RFC 2792. All X.509 key comparisons happen between normalized forms. A directly encoded RSA or DSA key and the same key inside an X.509 certificate therefore compare as equal.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole ID card is turned into a long string of letters and numbers. When KeyNote compares two cards, it only looks at the key printed on them, so a card and a bare key can still match.

sections.title: Signatures and Hash Functions
sections.content:
X.509 key identifier signatures are computed just like RSA or DSA signatures from RFC 2792. The difference is that the signer's public key is carried in an X.509 certificate in the Authorizer field. The RFC says these signatures exist for historical reasons and that implementers are encouraged to use the RSA- or DSA-based encodings instead.

The signature covers the assertion body, from the first keyword up to and including the newline before Signature:, plus the signature algorithm name including its trailing colon, such as sig-x509-sha512-base64:. It is encoded as an ASN.1 OCTET STRING and then written as hex or base64. The algorithm name has the form sig-x509-XXX-YYY:, where XXX is the hash function and YYY is hex or base64.

On hashes, X.509 signatures SHOULD support sha1 for backward compatibility. They MUST support sha256, sha512 and ripemd160. The same three hash keywords are also defined for RSA signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature is a seal on the rule. The seal can be made with several different fingerprint recipes. The old SHA1 recipe is still allowed for old systems, but newer, stronger recipes are required.

sections.title: Registered Identifiers
sections.content:
Following RFC 2792, IANA keeps a registry of reserved algorithm identifiers. This RFC reserves two public key format identifiers, x509-hex and x509-base64.

It also reserves fourteen signature algorithm identifiers: sha1, sha256, sha512 and ripemd160 variants of sig-x509- in both hex and base64 forms, plus sha256, sha512 and ripemd160 variants of sig-rsa- in both forms. The double quotes shown in the list are not part of the identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: The document puts new names on an official list so everyone uses the same labels for the same recipes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of credentials that use these keys depends directly on the strength of the public key algorithms involved. For the security of KeyNote itself, the RFC points to RFC 2704.

Validity of the certificate is not handled by KeyNote here: the application developer is responsible for ensuring that X.509 certificates are signed by a trusted authority, not expired, and not revoked. The use of SHA1 in signatures and key identifiers is discouraged because of weaknesses found in the algorithm in recent years.
sections.plainLanguage: An ID card is only as good as the check you make on it. The program using it must make sure the card is real, current and not cancelled, and should avoid the old, weak fingerprint recipe.
